name: HAProxy
summary: A high-performance proxy that schedules connection and stream work through event polling and task queues, separates transport and multiplexing layers, and balances work across threads and processes.

features.name: Event poller and prioritized task scheduler
features.description: HAProxy drives network progress from OS-specific polling and schedules timers, streams, and tasklets through per-thread run queues. Tasks carry ownership and wake-up state so work can be queued, expired, migrated, or handed to another thread when appropriate.
benefits: Handles many sockets without one blocking thread per connection
Makes timer expiry and runnable work explicit scheduling inputs
Allows urgent tasklets and ordinary tasks to receive different scheduling treatment
costs: Every protocol path must preserve readiness and wake-up invariants
Priorities and queue ownership make latency and fairness harder to reason about
A slow task can still consume a shared thread's execution budget

features.name: Layered connection, stream, and multiplexer state
features.description: HAProxy represents a logical stream separately from its connection and transport, and selects protocol multiplexers for frontend and backend sides. Connection ownership, readiness, shutdown, and mux callbacks form explicit boundaries between socket transport and proxy stream processing.
benefits: Separates reusable transport behavior from logical request or stream state
Supports multiple protocol muxes behind common connection operations
Provides lifecycle hooks for connection reuse, shutdown, and protocol upgrades
costs: State must stay consistent across stream, connection, transport, and mux layers
Protocol upgrades and half-closes create many partial-lifecycle cases
Debugging requires tracing ownership across several abstractions

features.name: Thread and process work distribution
features.description: HAProxy supports multi-threaded execution with thread-local contexts and cross-thread tasklets, while its master-worker documentation describes process supervision and seamless reload mechanisms. The proxy can therefore separate connection work, coordination, and replacement across execution boundaries.
benefits: Uses multiple CPUs while retaining thread-local scheduling structures
Supports operational replacement with reduced interruption during reload
Makes process and thread lifecycle responsibilities explicit
costs: Cross-thread wake-ups and shared state need synchronization
Reload and descriptor migration behavior adds operational state
The selected process and thread topology affects resource usage and latency

mathematical_views.question: How do socket readiness, timers, task priorities, and wake-ups select the next HAProxy work item?
assumptions: Each thread has a runnable queue and timer structure
Polling produces readiness events that wake connection or stream tasks
The view abstracts the implementation-specific poller while retaining task ownership

mathematical_views.question: Which stream, mux, transport, and socket states must agree for data to advance or a connection to close?
assumptions: Streams and connections are distinct vertices linked by ownership edges
Mux and transport layers expose readiness and shutdown transitions
The graph describes implementation boundaries rather than protocol correctness

mathematical_views.question: How does HAProxy move from one supervised process/thread topology to another while preserving eligible live work?
assumptions: A master or worker process owns lifecycle transitions
Descriptor and state transfer are explicit transition inputs
The view does not claim zero interruption for every protocol or failure mode

benefits: High connection concurrency with explicit readiness and timer scheduling
costs: Wake-up, priority, and task ownership rules increase scheduling complexity

benefits: Protocol reuse and separation of logical streams from sockets
costs: Partial shutdowns and cross-layer lifecycle ownership are difficult to validate

benefits: CPU scaling and operationally controlled reloads
costs: Synchronization, migration, and topology choices expand the failure surface
